headline: Hibiki, “echo”, is the continuative stem of the verb 響く (hibiku), “to echo”.
Chokuzen is Sinitic, built from 直 (choku, “direct, straight”) and 前 (zen, “front, forward; before”); the date of borrowing is unknown.
Takameru is the root of 高い (takai, “high, tall”) plus -meru, developed from the Classical Japanese verb 高む (takamu).
“To embrace” lost its first syllable: idaku shifted to daku.
Ayamari, “error”, is the continuative stem of the verb 誤る (ayamaru).
Shōmen is ultimately from Middle Chinese 正面, and is first attested in the early 1200s.
Yū, “superiority”, is from Middle Chinese 優.
Rajikase is a syllabic abbreviation of rajio kasetto, from English “radio cassette recorder”.
Kinyū is from Sinitic 記入, which Mandarin reads jìrù.
Yameru's etymology note is a single pointer: see 止める (yameru).
Keibi joins kei (警, “guard against”) and bi (備, “preparations”).
Kawase is an alteration of 交わし (kawashi, “an exchange”), from the verb 交わす (kawasu, “to exchange”).
Shinri is 心 (shin, “heart”) plus 理 (ri, “basic principle”).
Monji is from Middle Chinese 文字, literally “writing + character”.
Shōsū is 小 (shō, “small, little”) plus 数 (sū, “number”).
Chūshin comes from a Middle Chinese compound meaning literally “heart in the middle”.
Nikkori comes from nikori, “with a bright smile”, whose niko part is onomatopoeic for smiling.
Rusuban is 留守 (rusu, “absence”) plus 番 (ban, “watch”).
Katsugu is possibly a shift from katagu, or else a doublet of 被ぐ (katsugu).
Hazu has no settled origin, only several theories, one of them an abbreviation of 手はず (tehazu, “arrangement; plan”).
Dore is a shift from いずれ (izure), through idure and idore.
Pin is listed with three borrowings: Portuguese pinta (“a point, a mark”), English pin and English ping.
Suimen is 水 (sui, “water”) plus 面 (men, “surface”), two Sino-Xenic elements.
Ikari, “anger”, is the continuative stem of the verb 怒る (ikaru, “to get angry”).
